title: cash evidence without *pretending*
dek: Current demand supports testing one bounded lead-to-proposal workflow. The exact Farrice Cain offer remains unvalidated until a $750 deposit clears.
lens: buyer demand · supplier pricing · adoption · compliance

sections.heading: the evidence verdict
sections.body: Buyers are budgeting for lead qualification, follow-up, CRM integration, proposals, onboarding, and workflow assessment. Sellers list simple builds from the low hundreds through $1,500, while broader systems and assessments reach several thousand. Farrice's wedge is not raw automation; it is diagnosis, an acceptance test, human review, documentation, and final payment tied to demonstrated behavior.

rows.claim: Professional-service firms report use-case and expertise friction.
rows.evidence: RSM reports 47% naming lack of in-house expertise and 42% difficulty identifying the right AI use case.

rows.claim: SME use remains shallow in core activities.
rows.evidence: The OECD reports that only 29% of gen-AI-using SMEs use it in core business activities.

rows.claim: The exact offer is not proven.
rows.evidence: Marketplace budgets, supplier prices, reviews, and earnings establish category activity. They do not establish collected payment for Farrice's package.

items.why: Inquiry, qualification, proposal, and follow-up appear repeatedly across buyer demand and can be demonstrated in five days.
$1,500 is defended by diagnosis, tests, documentation, human hold, and acceptance-based payment—not by adding tools.
Real demand exists, but claim substantiation and regulatory boundaries raise proof and delivery burden.

sections.heading: the proof *boundary*
sections.body: No marketplace job post proves Farrice's offer sells. No seller claim proves buyer results. No demo proves adoption or revenue. The only validation event is a cleared $750 deposit for this exact scope.
